'''Linda Carol Hsieh-Wilson''' is an American chemist and the Milton and Rosalind Chang [[Professor]] of [[Chemistry]] at the [[California Institute of Technology]]. She is known for her work in chemical [[neuroscience|neurobiology]] on understanding the structure and function of carbohydrates in the nervous system.  Her studies have revealed critical roles for carbohydrates and protein glycosylation in fundamental processes ranging from cellular metabolism to memory storage. She is a member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences and was elected to the National Academy of Sciences in 2022.

== Biography ==
Hsieh-Wilson was born in New York City, NY and received her bachelor's degree in chemistry at Yale University, where she graduated magna cum laude. She then completed her Ph.D. in 1996 at the University of California, Berkeley, where she was a National Science Foundation Fellow in the laboratory of Peter G. Schultz and studied antibody-based catalysis.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://network.expertisefinder.com/experts/linda-hsieh-wilson|title=Linda Carol Hsieh-Wilson, California Institute of Technology: Learning and memory, Memory and motor control, Neurobiology • Expertise Finder Network|last=Finder|first=Expertise|website=network.expertisefinder.com|access-date=2017-05-02}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Hsieh-Wilson|first1=L. C.|last2=Schultz|first2=P. G.|last3=Stevens|first3=R. C.|date=1996-05-28|title=Insights into antibody catalysis: structure of an oxygenation catalyst at 1.9-angstrom resolution|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America|volume=93|issue=11|pages=5363–5367 |pmc=39251|pmid=8643580|doi=10.1073/pnas.93.11.5363|bibcode=1996PNAS...93.5363H|doi-access=free}}</ref> She then joined the lab of Professor and Nobel Prize Laureate [[Paul Greengard]] at Rockefeller University, where she characterized the protein phosphatase and actin-binding protein spinophilin<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Hsieh-Wilson|first1=L. C.|last2=Allen|first2=P. B.|last3=Watanabe|first3=T.|last4=Nairn|first4=A. C.|last5=Greengard|first5=P.|date=1999-04-06|title=Characterization of the neuronal targeting protein spinophilin and its interactions with protein phosphatase-1|journal=Biochemistry|volume=38|issue=14|pages=4365–4373|doi=10.1021/bi982900m |pmid=10194355}}</ref> and investigated its role in dendritic spines.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Grossman|first1=Stacie D.|last2=Hsieh-Wilson|first2=Linda C.|last3=Allen|first3=Patrick B.|last4=Nairn|first4=Angus C.|last5=Greengard|first5=Paul|date=2002-01-01|title=The actin-binding domain of spinophilin is necessary and sufficient for targeting to dendritic spines|journal=Neuromolecular Medicine|volume=2|issue=1|pages=61–69|doi=10.1385/NMM:2:1:61 |pmid=12230305|s2cid=21825701}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Hsieh-Wilson|first1=Linda C.|last2=Benfenati|first2=Fabio|last3=Snyder|first3=Gretchen L.|last4=Allen|first4=Patrick B.|last5=Nairn|first5=Angus C.|last6=Greengard|first6=Paul|date=2003-01-10|title=Phosphorylation of spinophilin modulates its interaction with actin filaments|journal=The Journal of Biological Chemistry|volume=278|issue=2|pages=1186–1194|doi=10.1074/jbc.M205754200 |pmid=12417592|s2cid=11557256|doi-access=free}}</ref> Hsieh-Wilson obtained an appointment in the Division of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering at the California Institute of Technology in 2000 as an assistant professor and became an investigator at the Howard Hughes Medical Institute in 2005. Hsieh-Wilson {{!}} www.cce.caltech.edu|website=www.cce.caltech.edu|language=en|access-date=2017-05-02|archive-date=2017-05-01|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170501231933/http://www.cce.caltech.edu/content/linda-c-hsieh-wilson|url-status=dead}}</ref>

== Research interests ==
===Overview===
Hsieh-Wilson's research is at the interface between [[organic chemistry]] and [[neuroscience]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.hhmi.org/research/investigators/hsieh-wilson.html |title=HHMI Scientist Abstract: Linda C. Hsieh-Wilson, Ph.D. |publisher=Howard Hughes Medical Institute |website= |access-date=2011-07-16}}</ref> She investigates how the [[Post-translational modification|post-translational addition]] of [[glycan]]s affect the structure and function of proteins in the [[nervous system]]. Her laboratory has developed a [[chemoenzymatic]] method to tag proteins that have been appended with a dynamic form of [[glycosylation]] called O-GlcNAc.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1038/nchembio881 |title=Probing the dynamics of O-GlcNAc glycosylation in the brain using quantitative proteomics |year=2007 |last1=Khidekel |first1=Nelly |last2=Ficarro |first2=Scott B |last3=Clark |first3=Peter M |last4=Bryan |first4=Marian C |last5=Swaney |first5=Danielle L |last6=Rexach |first6=Jessica E |last7=Sun |first7=Yi E |last8=Coon |first8=Joshua J |last9=Peters |first9=Eric C | display-authors = 8|journal=[[Nature Chemical Biology]] |volume=3 |issue=6 |pages=339–348 |pmid=17496889|url=https://authors.library.caltech.edu/56470/2/nchembio881-S1.pdf }}</ref> Her work with glycosaminoglycan microarrays has significantly advanced an understanding of specific sulfated glycosaminoglycans in [[neuronal communication]], learning, and memory as well as advanced the field of chemical biology.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1038/nchembio810 |title=Sulfation patterns of glycosaminoglycans encode molecular recognition and activity |year=2006 |last1=Gama |first1=Cristal I |last2=Tully |first2=Sarah E |last3=Sotogaku |first3=Naoki |last4=Clark |first4=Peter M |last5=Rawat |first5=Manish |last6=Vaidehi |first6=Nagarajan |last7=Goddard |first7=William A |last8=Nishi |first8=Akinori |last9=Hsieh-Wilson |first9=Linda C | display-authors = 8|journal=Nature Chemical Biology |volume=2 |issue=9 |pages=467–473 |pmid=16878128|s2cid=1229340 |url=https://authors.library.caltech.edu/56473/3/nchembio810-S2.pdf }}</ref> She has demonstrated how fucosylation can modulate neurite growth and neuronal morphology.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1126/stke.3172006tw472 |title=Sweet Memories of Synapsins? |year=2006 |journal=Science's STKE |volume=2006 |issue=317 |article-number=tw472|s2cid=220299653 }}</ref>

===O-GlcNAc Glycosylation===
Hsieh-Wilson and her colleagues have found that the covalent-modifications of intercellular proteins by [[O-GlcNAc|O-linked-N-acetylglucosamine (O-GlcNAc)]] within the mammalian nervous system have a large role in the regulation of gene expression, neuronal signaling, and synaptic plasticity.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Khidekel |first1=Nelly |last2=Ficarro |first2=Scott B. |last3=Peters |first3=Eric C. |last4=Hsieh-Wilson |first4=Linda C. |title=Exploring the O-GlcNAc proteome: Direct identification of O-GlcNAc-modified proteins from the brain |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |date=7 September 2004 |volume=101 |issue=36 |pages=13132–13137 |doi=10.1073/pnas.0403471101 |pmid=15340146 |pmc=516536 |bibcode=2004PNAS..10113132K |doi-access=free }}</ref> This [[post-translational modification]], has been analysed in the rat brain using a novel chemoenzymatic strategy wherein O-GlcNAc modified proteins are selectively labeled with fluorescent or [[biotin]] tags. This technique developed by Hsieh-Wilson and her lab has revealed over 200 O-GlcNAc modified proteins within the mammalian brain and such modifications have been shown to activate transcriptional function of proteins,<ref>http://apps.webofknowledge.com/full_record.do?product=WOS&search_mode=DaisyOneClickSearch&qid=11&SID=1AMO2etzAYAIFJZoUSG&page=1&doc=6&cacheurlFromRightClick=no{{dead link|date=January 2022}}</ref> regulate cancer metabolism,<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Hsieh-Wilson|first=Linda|date=2013-04-01|title=O-GlcNAc Signaling Regulates Cancer Metabolism |journal=The FASEB Journal|language=en|volume=27|issue=1 Supplement|article-number=452.2|doi=10.1096/fasebj.27.1_supplement.452.2 |doi-access=free}}</ref> regulate gene expression and memory formation,<ref>http://apps.webofknowledge.com/full_record.do?product=WOS&search_mode=DaisyOneClickSearch&qid=11&SID=1AMO2etzAYAIFJZoUSG&page=1&doc=21{{dead link|date=January 2022}}</ref> and carry out many other tasks in the brain and beyond.

===Glycosaminoglycans===
[[Glycosaminoglycan]]s are heterogeneously sulfated [[oligosaccharide]]s that are very important in nervous system development, spinal cord injury, inflammation and cancer [[metastasis]]. Hsieh-Wilson's research on this subject implicates the specific sulfation sequence of glycosaminoglycans as a way to modulate biological function. Specifically, her work with [[chondroitin sulfate]] (CS) and [[heparan sulfate]] (HS), the two most common glycosaminoglycans in the nervous system, has shown that this "sulfation code" functions as a molecular recognition element for growth factors and modulates neuronal growth,<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://www.nature.com/nchembio/journal/v2/n9/full/nchembio810.html|doi = 10.1038/nchembio810|title = Sulfation patterns of glycosaminoglycans encode molecular recognition and activity|year = 2006|last1 = Gama|first1 = Cristal I.|last2 = Tully|first2 = Sarah E.|last3 = Sotogaku|first3 = Naoki|last4 = Clark|first4 = Peter M.|last5 = Rawat|first5 = Manish|last6 = Vaidehi|first6 = Nagarajan|last7 = Goddard|first7 = William A.|last8 = Nishi|first8 = Akinori|last9 = Hsieh-Wilson|first9 = Linda C.|journal = Nature Chemical Biology|volume = 2|issue = 9|pages = 467–473|pmid = 16878128|s2cid = 1229340|url-access = subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Tully|first1=Sarah E.|last2=Mabon|first2=Ross|last3=Gama|first3=Cristal I.|last4=Tsai|first4=Sherry M.|last5=Liu|first5=Xuewei|last6=Hsieh-Wilson|first6=Linda C.|date=2004-06-01|title=A Chondroitin Sulfate Small Molecule that Stimulates Neuronal Growth|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|volume=126|issue=25|pages=7736–7737|doi=10.1021/ja0484045|pmid=15212495|bibcode=2004JAChS.126.7736T |issn=0002-7863|url=https://authors.library.caltech.edu/57662/2/ja0484045si20040423_071716_si.pdf}}</ref> indicating that these specific sulfated glycosaminoglycans play a major role in [[neuronal communication]], learning, and memory. Additionally, Hsieh-Wilson has elucidated the role of this sulfation in glycosaminoglycan-protein interaction using a carbohydrate [[Microarray analysis techniques|microarray]]-based approach developed in her lab.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Shipp|first1=Eric L.|last2=Hsieh-Wilson|first2=Linda C.|date=2007-02-01|title=Profiling the Sulfation Specificities of Glycosaminoglycan Interactions with Growth Factors and Chemotactic Proteins Using Microarrays|journal=Chemistry & Biology|volume=14|issue=2|pages=195–208|doi=10.1016/j.chembiol.2006.12.009|pmid=17317573|doi-access=free}}</ref>
